opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I think the hardest part was that almost nothing we expected going in turned out to be the real bottleneck.

When we started, the assumption in a lot of the field was that you'd collect a huge amount of supervised instruction data and that would carry you most of the way. What we found pretty quickly was that quality mattered far more than quantity. We ended up with something like tens of thousands of high-quality supervised examples rather than millions, and a model fine-tuned on that clean, carefully annotated set behaved noticeably better than one trained on a much bigger but noisier set. So a lot of the early challenge was setting up the annotation pipeline properly: vendor selection, guidelines, quality checks. That's not glamorous research work, but it's where much of the leverage was.

The second big challenge was RLHF itself, doing it at scale and iteratively. We weren't running one round of preference collection and calling it done. We'd collect human preferences, train reward models, improve the chat model, and then collect new preferences on the *new* model's outputs, because the reward model needs to stay on-distribution as the policy improves. Keeping that loop going week after week, with fresh data each time, was a big operational and scientific effort. We also had to balance two objectives that pull against each other, helpfulness and safety. That's why we trained separate reward models for each. If you push too hard on safety you get a model that refuses everything, and if you push too hard on helpfulness you get something that'll happily help with things it shouldn't. Finding that balance was a constant tension.

Then there were some subtler problems, like multi-turn consistency. If you tell the model at the start of a conversation, "always answer as a pirate" or "respond only in French," it tends to forget that after a few turns. We came up with a technique we called Ghost Attention to help the model keep track of the system instruction across the whole dialogue.

But if I had to pick one lesson, it's that I came in somewhat skeptical of RLHF. I thought supervised data from expert humans would be the gold standard. What changed my mind was seeing that the model, guided by human *preferences* rather than human *demonstrations*, could go beyond the quality of what the annotators themselves would write. Humans are much better at comparing two answers than at writing the perfect one, and RLHF exploits that. That was the real "aha" for me.

r001.rationale: The response names data quality, annotation operations, iterative RLHF, safety-helpfulness balance, and multi-turn consistency as challenges. It does not identify a lack of research guidance at large scale as the principal challenge.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, the hardest part wasn't the modeling, it was the data. When we started, we had this assumption that you need millions of instruction examples, and we collected a lot of third-party SFT data. But when we looked at it closely, the quality was all over the place. And what we found is that a few tens of thousands of really high-quality, human-written examples beat millions of noisy ones. That was counterintuitive for a lot of people internally, because scale is the religion in pretraining. But in alignment, quality dominates.

The second thing, and this is maybe the one I'd emphasize most, is that we underestimated RLHF. Coming from the academic world, a lot of us thought RLHF was a bit of a hack, something you do at the end to polish. What we saw was the opposite. Once SFT gets the model to a reasonable place, humans can't really write better answers than the model anymore, but they can still tell which of two answers is better. That comparison signal is much cheaper and much more reliable than asking someone to write the ideal response. So the reward model becomes the real bottleneck. We spent an enormous amount of effort there: separate reward models for helpfulness and safety, iterating weekly batches of preference data, making sure the data distribution tracked the current policy and not a model from two months ago.

And then at scale, the operational side is brutal. You're coordinating annotation vendors, you're dealing with distribution shift in your preference data each iteration, you're trying to detect reward hacking before it shows up in the final model. Things like the model becoming overly cautious, refusing benign requests, because the safety reward was easier to game than the helpfulness one. We had to actively balance that.

So if I had to summarize: data quality over quantity, RLHF is not optional, and iterate fast with fresh human feedback. Those three lessons cost us a lot to learn.

r001.rationale: The response identifies data quality, RLHF, and operational challenges as the main difficulties. It does not identify a lack of research guidance at large scale as the principal challenge.

astra-6.text:
I’d say the hardest part is defining what good instruction-following actually means, and then making sure your training signal captures it. A response can look helpful and still miss what the user asked. It can follow the wording very closely and miss the intent. And sometimes the right behavior is to ask a clarifying question.

At scale, that becomes a feedback problem. You need consistent judgments across a very diverse set of requests, and you need evaluations that tell you whether you’re improving the assistant rather than just making its answers sound better. There’s also a balance between helpfulness and safety: you want the model to handle difficult requests appropriately without refusing perfectly reasonable ones.

So I’d frame the challenge as getting that whole feedback loop right—what you collect, what you reward, and how you check that the improvement generalizes.

r001.rationale: The response frames the main challenge as defining and evaluating instruction-following feedback at scale; it does not identify a lack of research guidance as the principal challenge.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the hardest part was defining what a good answer actually is. With pretraining, you have a relatively clear objective: predict the next token. With instruction following, you’re asking people to judge whether an answer is helpful, accurate, safe—and those judgments can conflict.

At scale, that becomes a data-quality problem as much as a modeling problem. You need consistent feedback across very different requests, and you need to make sure the model is learning to help the user rather than just learning the style of answers that get high ratings. A longer, more confident answer can look better without actually being better.

So the challenge is the iteration loop: train the model, examine where it fails, collect feedback that addresses those failures, and repeat. You can improve a benchmark and still make the experience worse in some conversations. Getting that balance right is much harder than simply adding more instruction examples.

r001.rationale: The response identifies defining and consistently evaluating good answers, feedback quality, and iteration as the main challenges. It does not identify a lack of research guidance at large scale as the principal challenge.
